\chapter{Hable Usted --- The Polite Command}
\label{ch:command-usted}
\hlchaptermodality{129}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give a formal command and say why the usted form is the polite one.}

Complete ES-C50-hable-usted: produce hable por favor and explain why the usted command is polite.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hable usted]{hable usted — the polite command}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-hable-usted}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Usted} takes the \textbf{he/she} form of every verb. You have known that since you learned it. Watch what that does to a command.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the subjunctive, a third time}]
\begin{quote}
A command to \emph{usted} — positive or negative — uses the \textbf{subjunctive}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Hable}, por favor.} — Speak, please. \emph{\textbf{Coma}, por favor.} — Eat, please. \emph{\textbf{No hable.}} — Don't speak.
\end{quote}

So the subjunctive now covers three of the four boxes:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{\emph{tú}} & \textbf{\emph{usted}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{do it} & \emph{habla} — ordinary present & \emph{\textbf{hable}} — subjunctive \\
\textbf{don't} & \emph{no hables} — subjunctive & \emph{no hable} — subjunctive \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One box out of four uses an ordinary form, and it is the informal, positive one. Everything else reaches for the subjunctive.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Here is why the formal command is the polite one, and it is not because the subjunctive is a fancy form.

Remember what \emph{usted} is: a worn-down \textbf{vuestra merced}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace\textquotedblright{} — a \textbf{title}, and titles are third person. That is why \emph{usted} takes he/she endings. So a command to \emph{usted} is not grammatically aimed at the person in front of you at all. It is aimed at \emph{your grace}, spoken about rather than to.

That indirectness \textbf{is} the politeness. Every polite language does some version of it: you soften an order by not pointing it straight at somebody. English does it with extra words — \emph{could you possibly}, \emph{would you mind} — where Spanish does it with a verb form and a fossil of a title.

Which means that if the \emph{usted} command ever feels stiff to you, you are hearing it correctly. It is supposed to hold somebody at a small distance.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Habla\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Hable, por favor\textquotedblright{} — hear the distance open up
  \item all four boxes: \textquotedblleft{}habla, no hables, hable, no hable\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}Speak, please,\textquotedblright{} to \emph{usted}? (\emph{\textbf{Hable, por favor}}.) Which form? (The \textbf{subjunctive} again.) Why is it polite? (Because \emph{usted} is a \textbf{title} — the order is aimed past the person, not at them.) Next: all four in one place.
\end{tcolorbox}
